name: Red light therapy for eyes

lead: Red light therapy uses low-power red or near-infrared lights placed near the skin. Some looksmaxxing lists suggest using it around the eyes for a brighter, fresher eye area.

The suggested mechanism is light absorbed by an enzyme in mitochondria, which is thought to boost cell energy and circulation, though Wikipedia describes the effect as under investigation. The eye research cited in reference material concerns repeated low-level red-light treatment for juvenile myopia, a different goal. No study of cosmetic brightening of the eye area was found.

paras: People use LED masks, wands or panels held near the face for short sessions several times a week, over weeks. Some devices come with eye shields.
Mild irritation is reported, long-term effects are unknown, and eye protection is suggested for some devices. Ocular safety for cosmetic use is not established in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Users shine red light around the eyes in the hope that boosted cell energy and circulation leaves the eye area looking brighter and fresher. The eye research that exists concerns childhood myopia, not cosmetic effects.

lead: Red light therapy, also called low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, applies low-power red or near-infrared light from lasers or LEDs to the body. Wikipedia describes its effectiveness as under investigation and notes that the generally accepted theory involves an enzyme in mitochondria.[1]

In looksmaxxing lists the entry is framed as a way to brighten the eye area, with emerging evidence. No clinical study of red light for cosmetic brightening of the eyes was found. Ocular research cited on Wikipedia concerns juvenile myopia, where repeated low-level red-light treatment has been studied in children.[1]

paras: Photobiomodulation uses low-power lasers or LEDs at specific wavelengths applied to the surface of the body, and some devices have US FDA clearance for particular uses.[1]

According to Wikipedia, evidence is tentative for some musculoskeletal pain, effective for preventing oral mucositis in certain transplant patients, and mixed for hair loss.[1] The article says low-level red light may be effective for juvenile myopia and cites a 2022 study on repeated low-level red-light therapy in children.[1]

Wikipedia reports occasional mild pain or skin irritation, unknown long-term effects, and suggests eye protection for some devices.[1] Devices for ocular use are a separate consideration from skin devices.
No studies found for cosmetic brightening of the eyes or under-eye area. Related research on red-light therapy for myopia in children and other conditions is summarised on Wikipedia.[1]
